title: Generative AI and the Future of Legal Scholarship (June 2026 Edition)
author: Andrew M. Perlman

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI writing: Present gains can weaken future judgment
st.an: The source shifts the debate from how supervised AI writing should preserve judgment and competence to a more fundamental institutional question: what legal scholarship is for when competent scholarly output can be generated at near-zero marginal cost. It acknowledges hallucinations but treats them as secondary, without substantively addressing verification costs, developmental loss, or independent competence assessment.
qs: This Article argues that the question cannot be answered from within the conceptual scheme that produced it.

st.t: Citation errors: Genuine authorities can still mislead
st.an: The source accepts that hallucinated legal material requires engineering improvements and stricter human verification, but argues that citation accuracy is not the fundamental institutional problem. It redirects attention from misleading authorities and verification duties to whether even flawless AI-generated scholarship can evidence the named author’s understanding.
qs: A hallucinated brief is an epistemic failure, correctable by better engineering and stricter verification.

But a flawless machine-written article—every citation real, every pincite accurate—does not restore the artifact regime; it completes the regime's collapse, because it severs, perfectly and undetectably, the link between textual competence and authorial cognition that the regime existed to certify.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The source accepts that verification and sanctions address hallucinated or counterfeit legal content, but argues that this governance frame misses a more fundamental problem in legal scholarship: even perfectly accurate AI-generated writing cannot evidence the purported author’s understanding. It therefore redirects attention from inquiry failures and citation integrity to the institutional evidentiary role of authorship.
qs: Note the precise irony of the sanctions opinions: what they punish is counterfeiting the regime's currency— the fixed, checkable citation—and so they police the artifact's apparatus while its evidentiary foundation dissolves beneath them.78 The hallucination literature measures the machines against the regime's standards of verification.

st.t: Human oversight: Accountability is not effective control
st.an: The source does not directly assess whether human oversight provides effective control, independent verification or adequate professional accountability. Instead, it shifts the governance focus toward corpus stewardship, provenance and open evaluation as system-level mechanisms for maintaining integrity and contesting failures in AI-mediated legal scholarship.
qs: If a public corpus can be poisoned cheaply,152 then curation—provenance, authentication, the keeping of the record—becomes to the latent regime what the great reporters were to the print one: the unglamorous work on which everything downstream silently depends.

Open evaluation inverts the artifact regime's asymmetry of standing: under the old regime, an outsider's critique needed placement, patronage, letterhead; under open benchmarks, a documented failure is a failure whoever files it, and the registry cannot see the provenance of a counterexample.

st.t: Legal assistance: Lower cost complicates protection boundaries
st.an: The source does not directly address how cheaper legal assistance should expand access to justice while preserving consumer protection and accountability. It instead redirects attention to how near-zero-cost, competent AI-generated legal prose changes the evidentiary value of scholarly artifacts, while acknowledging hallucinations and sanctions as practical risks.
qs: The technical fact sufficient for everything that follows is narrow and undisputed: next-token prediction at scale now produces competent, genre-conforming, argumentative legal prose, in unlimited quantity, on demand, at a marginal cost approaching zero.
2023) (sanctioning attorneys who filed ChatGPT-fabricated opinions and cataloguing the "[m]any harms" that "flow from the submission of fake opinions").

st.t: Legal reliability: Mitigation cannot eliminate verification
st.an: The source acknowledges substantial, task-dependent hallucination risks and current verification duties, but rejects reliability as the decisive or durable issue. It redirects attention from whether mitigation can eliminate verification to the loss of scholarship’s authorship-certification function, arguing that even perfectly reliable machine-written work would sever the link between textual competence and human cognition.
qs: It fails first on its own empirical terms, because reliability is an engineering parameter on a steep improvement slope—the gap between the 2024 profile and the 2025 retrieval-augmented results is itself the trend line—and no durable institutional settlement should be built on a parameter.77 It fails second, and more fundamentally, because it mistakes the nature of the crisis.

But a flawless machine-written article—every citation real, every pincite accurate—does not restore the artifact regime; it completes the regime's collapse, because it severs, perfectly and undetectably, the link between textual competence and authorial cognition that the regime existed to certify.

st.t: Legal workflows: Immediate gains create competence risks
st.an: The source acknowledges rapid capability gains and citation uncertainty, but its principal argument shifts away from supervised legal workflows and lawyer competence toward a different institutional problem: abundant AI-generated scholarship dissolves the scarcity and credentialing function of the law-review article. It therefore reframes the disruption rather than directly accepting the cluster’s workflow-centred proposition.
qs: Generative artificial intelligence does not merely assist this system.

st.t: Case teaching: Useful method became restrictive default
st.an: The source extends the cluster’s critique beyond case teaching by showing that legal education’s broader institutional forms supply training and knowledge functions the case method does not fully provide. Its account of student-editor verification and the article’s bundled functions materially develops the cluster’s institutional explanation, though it does not itself advocate curricular reform.
qs: The student editors received an immersion in sources and a discipline of verification that the case method itself never quite delivered, at a price—their labor—the schools were pleased to accept.
Four Functions, One Form      The settlement endured for fourteen decades because the artifact fused four functions that have no necessary connection to one another.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s core claims that AI can make bounded legal production abundant while verification, human normative judgment and institutional design remain decisive. It materially extends them within legal scholarship by proposing a redesigned operating model—maintained normative systems, open evaluation and corpus governance—rather than treating AI as an isolated writing tool. Its stronger claim that the article is no longer scholarship’s principal unit goes beyond, but does not reject, the cluster’s work-redesign proposition.
qs: The reorientation—of units, of measures, of institutions—is what this Article calls latent scholarship.

The human remainder is therefore not a residue but a constitution: choosing the problems, warranting the confidence, standing behind the positions, designing the commons—and tending the nomos, for Cover's communities of meaning do not dissolve into the machines; they acquire,        See supra notes 41–42 and accompanying text.

kp.k: Single-prompt experiment reports stronger scholarship, with unverified citations
kp.d: Perlman's preface reports that Claude Fable 5 (Max) drafted the article on June 9, 2026, from one prompt in less than an hour, producing 178 footnotes. He judges the ideas and prose stronger than his late-2024 experiment, which required multiple prompts. Subsequent requests converted endnotes to footnotes and asked the model to verify citations, resulting in seven footnote edits. Perlman did not independently confirm every citation and explicitly allows for hallucinated references; this is a demonstration and personal assessment, not a controlled evaluation of scholarly quality. The substantive theory below belongs to the AI-generated article.
qs: Another notable advance is the generation of 178 footnotes.
Although I have not confirmed the accuracy of each citation (i.e. there may be hallucinated references), a spot check suggests that many of the footnotes stand for the proposition cited.
It edited seven of the footnotes.

kp.k: Cheap argument generation undermines scholarship's traditional credential
kp.d: The generated article argues that the law-review article historically bundled discovery, communication, credentialing and archiving because competent legal argument was scarce, fixed and attributable. Its central theoretical claim is that generative AI breaks the inference from competent text to the author's intellectual work—the 'Menard problem'—and therefore threatens article-based hiring, tenure, prestige and scholarly authority, rather than merely accelerating drafting.
qs: The article bundled four functions—discovery, communication, credentialing, and archiving
The artifact's crisis is evidentiary, not epistemic.
What has ended is not the human element in legal thought. What has ended is the use of prose as its proof.

kp.k: Competence evidence supports the article's proposed structural rupture
kp.d: The article cites GPT-4's reported ninetieth-percentile Uniform Bar Examination performance, while acknowledging a persuasive cohort-based correction that left passage intact. It reports that late-2022 ChatGPT earned a C+ across four real law-school examinations and that subsequent controlled studies found assistance benefits concentrated among weaker students. These reported studies underpin its argument that mechanically attainable median competence weakens text-based credentialing; the article does not present a direct controlled test establishing median law-review quality.
qs: the comparison cohort flattered the machine—but the contest concerned rank, not passage, and the correction left the qualitative result intact.
In late 2022, ChatGPT took four real law school examinations and earned a C+
The artifact regime never certified genius; it certified competence.

kp.k: Hallucinations require verification but do not resolve credentialing
kp.d: The article reports legal hallucination research on general-purpose models using 2023 data and a successor study of retrieval-augmented commercial legal research tools, alongside Mata and subsequent sanctions incidents and ABA Formal Opinion 512. It argues that even flawless, verified machine-written scholarship would further sever text from authorial cognition. Its characterization of reliability as rapidly improving is an asserted interpretation of the cited studies, not a new longitudinal measurement.
qs: even retrieval-augmented commercial research tools—systems engineered specifically to suppress confabulation—still hallucinated at rates no lawyer could ethically ignore.
the organized bar has layered duties of verification atop the existing competence rules.
a flawless machine-written article—every citation real, every pincite accurate—does not restore the artifact regime

kp.k: Authorship authentication cannot preserve the old scholarly system
kp.d: The article criticizes disclosure mandates, human-authorship certifications, detection and watermarking on technical, conceptual and functional grounds. It cites detection brittleness and paraphrase evasion, describes human–AI production as a continuum, and argues that provenance cannot restore text as evidence of cognition. It also criticizes enthusiastic AI-assisted production that retains the article as the unit of scholarship, while acknowledging authentication's short-term hygienic value.
qs: Disclosure regimes presuppose a discrete event called "use of AI," a moment that occurred or did not and can therefore be reported. Production does not have that shape anymore.
Provenance was a proxy for cognition
The accelerationists and the authenticators are thus two wings of a single conservatism

kp.k: Latent scholarship relocates value into four scarce functions
kp.d: The article proposes 'latent scholarship': as lawyers and judges increasingly obtain arguments through models, scholarly work should focus on formulation of consequential questions, validation of claims and systems, human commitment to normative positions, and architecture of corpora, models and benchmarks. It treats LegalBench and legal hallucination audits as prototypes of this shift, while maintaining that normative responsibility belongs to people and communities rather than models.
qs: When competent argumentative text becomes free, four goods remain scarce, and together they define the new discipline.
The second is validation.
The third is commitment. A model can state every position and occupies none.
The fourth is architecture

kp.k: Maintained normative systems would replace articles as scholarly units
kp.d: The proposed replacement is a queryable, versioned legal framework comprising a normative specification, curated corpus, implementation, benchmark suite, public failure log and signed commitment statement. The article imagines a scholar building 'Cathedral-1' in 2030 and a clerk comparing version 1.7 with a rival in 2031. These are illustrative future scenarios, not deployed systems. The proposal emphasizes contestable rival frameworks, not automated convergence on one correct law, and allows prose scholarship to persist without remaining the dominant unit of credit.
qs: Call it the maintained normative system: a framework for some region of law, stated with operational precision and kept alive over time.
Authorship becomes maintainership.
latent scholarship is constitutively pluralist, a marketplace of maintained nomoi whose disagreements are precise, queryable, and never final.

kp.k: Scholarly influence would track changes in model behavior
kp.d: The article proposes 'uptake delta' as an alternative to citation counts: the contribution-attributable change in systems actually consulted by the profession. It suggests influence functions, ablation and behavioral probing as measurement approaches, describing measurement as possible in principle and increasingly in practice. It also anticipates optimization for ingestion, corpus poisoning and Goodhart-style gaming, recommending plural metrics, rotating partially sealed evaluation sets and adversarial audits rather than claiming any metric is manipulation-proof.
qs: Define the uptake delta: the change in the behavior of the systems the profession actually consults that is attributable to a scholarly contribution.
There will be model optimization—the search-engine optimization of scholarship
The answer is not a Goodhart-proof metric, which does not exist, but a Goodhart-resistant institution.

kp.k: Law reviews and tenure would reward evaluation and maintenance
kp.d: As institutional proposals explicitly framed as imagination rather than a blueprint, law reviews would shift from article selection toward curating hard-case benchmarks, adversarially evaluating systems, publishing failures and periodically retesting. The article treats students' existing source-checking and hypothetical-construction skills as foundations for this role. Tenure would assess portfolios of formulations, benchmark and audit work, defended commitments, corpus stewardship and system maintenance rather than bibliographies and journal prestige.
qs: It is offered as institutional imagination rather than blueprint
Article selection was never what law reviews did distinctively well; verification was.
A tenure file in the latent regime is a portfolio rather than a bibliography

kp.k: Courts should scrutinize normative systems through a Daubert analogy
kp.d: The article proposes adapting Daubert-style scrutiny to machine-mediated scholarly arguments: benchmarks for testability, audit records for error rates, adversarial review for peer review and uptake for acceptance. Opposing parties could request failure logs and rerun relevant cases. This is a proposed framework, not a statement that existing evidence law already governs these systems. Drawing on technological due process and black-box critiques, it calls for inspectability while distinguishing systems advising judges from systems judging people.
qs: A prose article could never be Dauberted. A system can.
the opposing party can demand the failure log, rerun the contested class of cases, and impeach the system the way one impeaches an expert: on its record.
those systems judged persons, these advise judges

kp.k: Open legal corpora become essential institutional infrastructure
kp.d: The article argues that public legal materials, open case-law projects and Pile of Law become foundational infrastructure for scholarship and legal knowledge systems. It warns that proprietary intermediation, concentrated frontier-model ownership and corpus poisoning could place legal knowledge under corporate control. Recommendations include commons stewardship, provenance tracking and 'epistemic antitrust' focused on ownership of the knowledge substrate. It acknowledges that a commons is necessary but insufficient to prevent infrastructural exclusion.
qs: If frontier systems are few, proprietary, and corporately aligned, latent scholarship collapses into company scholarship: the nomos acquires a landlord.
The response this Article urges is an epistemic antitrust—structural attention to who owns the substrate of legal knowledge
the commons of Part V.D is necessary rather than sufficient.

kp.k: Copyright doctrine is interpreted as supporting scholarly commons
kp.d: The article reads human-authorship doctrine and Copyright Office guidance as locating protectable contributions in human selection, arrangement, direction and creative control rather than autonomous generated text. It combines this with section 102(b)'s exclusion of systems and methods of operation to argue that maintained normative systems tend toward commons-based organization. The commons implication is the article's theoretical interpretation of the cited doctrine, not a reported judicial ruling on its proposed scholarly format.
qs: Read affirmatively, it is a map of where protectable contribution now lives: in selection, arrangement, direction, and creative control
Section 102(b) withholds protection from any system or method of operation as such
Authorship doctrine, asked to police the old regime's border, has quietly chartered the new one.

kp.k: Human normative judgment remains central despite executable frameworks
kp.d: Answering objections about machine understanding and revived Langdellian scientism, the article treats AI systems as media for human normative argument rather than scholars. It concedes that benchmarks embody contestable values and that legal concerns resist a single metric, proposing rival systems, plural metrics and contestable benchmarks. Human responsibilities remain choosing problems, warranting confidence, defending positions and governing infrastructure; model-generated predictions do not themselves settle what law ought to be.
qs: A distribution cannot answer a normative question; it can only inform the one who must.
The system is the medium of normative argument, not its author
Metrics are plural by constitution, benchmarks are contestable objects of scholarship

kp.k: Model collapse and skill homogenization constrain the proposed transition
kp.d: The article cites measured degradation from recursive training on generated data and correlated error from shared systems. It reports mixed findings from an April 5, 2026 working paper: early assistance improved later unaided legal reasoning, but machine-aided revision pulled the strongest performers toward the mean. It recommends fresh human contributions, provenance-tracked corpora, rival maintained systems and pedagogical sequencing rather than blanket abstention. It treats these risks as design constraints, not as resolved problems.
qs: Models trained recursively on machine output degrade—collapse is now measured, not conjectured

early machine assistance in a legal-reasoning task did not erode later unaided performance—the assisted group did better even after the tool was withdrawn—but machine-aided revision dragged the strongest performers toward the mean.
the pedagogical answer is sequencing rather than abstention

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Perlman reports improved AI production of legal scholarship; the AI-generated article develops a broader prediction that scholarly value will migrate from authored articles to maintained, executable legal frameworks.
pts.d: Attribution is important: Perlman's own preface describes and assesses a drafting experiment, while the substantive thesis appears in the article he identifies as generated by Claude Fable 5 (Max). Perlman says the June 2026 output has stronger ideas and prose than his late-2024 experiment and required only one substantive drafting prompt. The generated article argues that inexpensive, on-demand production of competent legal argument breaks the inference from polished text to a human author's intellectual work, undermining the article's credentialing function. It predicts that discovery, communication, credentialing and archiving will decouple from the fixed article. It rejects authorship authentication and disclosure as a durable solution, arguing that even perfect provenance would not restore the article's former evidentiary role. Its proposed successor is 'latent scholarship': human work concentrated on formulation of important questions, validation of claims and systems, accountable normative commitment, and architecture of corpora, models and benchmarks. Its proposed unit is a 'maintained normative system' comprising a normative specification, curated corpus, implementation, benchmark suite, public failure log and signed commitment statement. Rival systems would make legal theories interrogable and disagreements observable across shared hypotheticals. Scholarly influence would increasingly consist of changing the behavior of systems used by lawyers and judges rather than accumulating citations. Institutional proposals include law reviews becoming recurring evaluation and certification bodies, tenure portfolios emphasizing system contributions and measurable uptake, courts scrutinizing normative systems through a Daubert-like framework, and public stewardship of legal corpora. These are predictions and institutional proposals, not reports of completed institutional change. The text expressly distinguishes its thesis from lawyer displacement and from convergent, fully automated adjudication: humans retain responsibility for normative choices, and rival interpretations remain central.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source combines a disclosed drafting demonstration, cited capability and reliability studies, examples of judicial use, and theoretical analogies; its proposed institutional future is not empirically demonstrated.
pts.d: Perlman's direct evidence is a single experiment dated June 9, 2026: a draft with 178 footnotes, generated in less than an hour, followed by conversion to Word footnotes and a model citation-verification request that changed seven footnotes. His quality comparison with late 2024 is expressly personal judgment. He did not independently confirm every citation and reports only a spot check, so the generated article's authorities should be recorded as evidence it offers rather than independently verified support. For capability, the generated article cites GPT-4 bar-exam research, acknowledges a published challenge to the claimed ninetieth-percentile ranking while retaining the passing-result claim, and cites law-school examinations and controlled studies reporting gains from AI assistance, especially for weaker students, plus quality and productivity gains in simulated practice. It invokes Perlman's 2024 experiment and Conklin and Houston's 2025 working paper on statistical indications of increasing AI drafting in published legal scholarship; no numerical adoption estimate is supplied. For reliability, it cites Dahl and colleagues' study of 2023-era public models and Magesh and colleagues' study of retrieval-augmented professional legal research tools. It treats lower but persistent errors in the latter as evidence of improvement. Court sanctions incidents, including Mata, are separate examples of fabricated-authority harms, not measured error rates; ABA Formal Opinion 512 supplies professional-duty authority. The Newsom concurrence in Snell is offered as an example of judicial engagement with model-assisted interpretation, not evidence that courts have adopted maintained normative systems. LegalBench is presented as a working academic prototype for benchmark-based scholarship; influence-function research supports the proposed measurement of scholarly uptake. Borges, Cover, legal realism, copyright doctrine and Daubert provide conceptual or legal analogies. For risks, the article cites research on recursively generated training data, algorithmic monoculture, corpus poisoning and a 2026 legal-reasoning experiment reporting mixed effects on later unaided performance. No implemented Cathedral system, uptake-based tenure regime or court screening program is evaluated.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The article presents the competence shift as already underway by June 2026, illustrates institutional change in 2030–2031, and makes the transition conditional on human accountability, pluralism, reliable evaluation and accessible infrastructure.
pts.d: The preface compares June 2026 generation with a late-2024 demonstration. The article locates the technical origins in transformers in 2017 and scaling and foundation-model developments in 2020–2022, asserting that the old exclusive link between competent prose and trained human cognition lasted until approximately 2022. It describes current legal scholarship and professional use as already affected, rather than giving a future date for first capability. Its example of a scholar building Cathedral-1 in 2030 and a clerk consulting version 1.7 in 2031 is illustrative, not a deployment commitment. It predicts that an academy relying on authorship authentication will face an emptied-out certification practice 'within a decade.' Most institutional changes have no firm deadline. The competence claim concerns median, genre-conforming argument rather than a demonstration that models reliably produce exceptional scholarship. It does not depend on machines understanding language or holding beliefs. Persistent hallucinations and human verification duties remain acknowledged. The proposed future requires humans to formulate worthwhile questions, warrant confidence, commit to normative positions and govern infrastructure. It also requires contestable benchmarks, rival maintained systems, disclosed evaluation records and protection against corpus poisoning, metric gaming and concentration. The article concedes that open corpora are necessary but insufficient to address unequal infrastructure power. It anticipates continued prose scholarship as an art and practice, while predicting its loss of central credentialing status.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The primary affected domain is the legal academy, with downstream consequences for courts, practicing lawyers, infrastructure providers and communities whose legal perspectives enter—or are excluded from—AI systems.
pts.d: Scholars would shift from producing discrete articles to maintaining frameworks, constructing tests, curating corpora and publicly defending normative commitments. Hiring and tenure committees would assess contribution portfolios and uptake rather than predominantly journal placement and citations. Student law-review editors would move from checking textual authorities toward benchmark construction, adversarial evaluation and repeated certification of systems; the article treats their training in hypotheticals as relevant expertise. Law students, particularly weaker performers, are described as benefiting from AI assistance in cited studies, while stronger performers may face homogenizing effects during AI-assisted revision. Judges, clerks and practicing lawyers would encounter scholarly ideas through queryable models and comparisons between rival systems. Opposing litigants would be able to challenge a relied-upon system using its evaluation record and failure log; judicial responsibility is not transferred to a model. Libraries, open-law projects and corpus stewards gain an infrastructure-governance role. Proprietary model owners could acquire disproportionate power over legal knowledge, especially where capital, English-language material and documented traditions dominate training. Outsider scholars and smaller normative communities could gain opportunities through open counterexample submission and community-maintained systems, although the article concedes persistent resource inequality. The public is affected indirectly through the transparency, diversity and accountability of systems informing legal authority. The document does not offer concrete predictions about law-firm staffing, provider market shares, legal-service prices or the civil justice gap.
